textRun.content: Identity-based habits

An identity-based habit starts with the kind of person I want to become, not just an outcome. Each small action is evidence for that identity. A person who wants to be a reader can start by reading one page after breakfast.
My interpretation: one missed day is not a verdict on identity. Return to the next small action instead of treating a lapse as proof of failure.
Goals and systems

A goal describes a desired result; a system is the repeated process that makes progress possible. My goal is to finish twelve books this year. My system is to read for ten minutes after breakfast and leave a book on the table.
Goals give direction, but a repeatable system matters on ordinary days. Winning once does not show that a process is sustainable.
Motivation and friction

Motivation varies from day to day, so my plan should not depend on feeling inspired. Reduce the effort needed to begin: put the exercise shoes by the door and choose a short route before the morning arrives.
Friction is the effort between intention and action. Adding friction can discourage an unwanted habit: log out of the video app and put the remote in a drawer.
Habit stacking
Attach a new action to an existing routine with a specific cue: after I pour my morning tea, I will read one paragraph. The established action makes the new action easier to remember.
The cue must actually happen at the right time and place. Attaching evening stretching to an unpredictable phone call is less reliable than attaching it to brushing my teeth.
Environment design

Visible cues make helpful actions easier to notice. Keep a filled water bottle on the desk and place the guitar on a stand where I will see it. Put distracting devices in another room during focused work.

Environment design changes what is obvious around me; friction changes how much effort an action takes. A visible book is an environmental cue, while opening it to the bookmarked page removes a small starting cost.
The two-minute start
Shrink the first step until starting feels easy: put on walking shoes instead of promising a long workout. Starting small is an entry ritual, not a rule forbidding a longer session.
My experiment is to write one sentence after opening the laptop. On busy days that sentence counts; on other days I may keep writing.
Tracking and recovery
A simple checkmark records that I showed up, but the measure should not replace the purpose. Counting pages is useful only if I still understand what I read.
After a missed day, resume at the next planned opportunity. Review the obstacle without moral judgment. If the cue failed repeatedly, redesign the routine.
Weekly experiment

For the next week I will place a book beside the kettle, read one paragraph after pouring tea, and mark a calendar. At the end of the week I will ask whether the cue was reliable and the action small enough.
These are my personal learning notes. They contain no sales figures, publication date, neuroscience claims, or biography of the author.
